articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Issues New General Licenses, and Amends FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended existing Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide further guidance on these actions.

In addition to the Iran-related actions, OFAC also announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. These removals indicate a recalibration of sanctions in these areas, though specific details of the removed entities were not immediately available.

The issuance of new General Licenses and amended FAQs aims to clarify the scope of the new designations and provide authorized avenues for certain transactions, helping to ensure that legitimate humanitarian and other permitted activities can continue without undue disruption.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations Targeting Intellectual Property Theft, Issues General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These actions target entities involved in the theft of American intellectual property, a critical national security and economic concern for the United States.

Alongside these designations, OFAC issued associated General Licenses to mitigate unintended consequences and ensure that legitimate activities are not unduly impacted. The PAIPA designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to protecting American innovation and technology from illicit acquisition.

Beijing has expressed strong opposition to the U.S. sanctions on five Chinese companies linked to a former Google engineer accused of intellectual property theft. China's commerce ministry stated that the move 'severely harms the legitimate rights and interests' of Chinese businesses and urged the U.S. to 'correct its erroneous practice,' without specifying countermeasures.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / AP / Global Times

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and an updated Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026. This action aims to refine existing sanctions policies concerning Venezuela.

The amendment to the General License and the updated FAQ provide further clarity and guidance to individuals and entities engaging in transactions related to Venezuela. These adjustments are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to ensure that sanctions remain targeted and effective while minimizing unintended humanitarian or economic impacts.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related and Cuba designations on October 15, 2026. These actions target entities deemed to be involved in activities contrary to U.S. foreign policy and national security interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses, along with updated Frequently Asked Questions. These accompanying measures are intended to provide clarity and guidance to the public regarding the scope of the sanctions and permissible transactions.

One Hong Kong entity, Elitesphere Trading Co. Limited, was sanctioned for its alleged ties to Iran, specifically for moving funds through a clandestine banking system to support Iranian sanctions evasion.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action signifies a recalibration of sanctions against individuals or entities previously targeted under the Venezuela sanctions program.

Designation removals typically occur when the sanctioned party has met certain conditions, or when the U.S. government determines that the designation no longer serves its foreign policy objectives. Further details regarding the specific entity removed were not immediately provided.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing activities globally.

These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to disrupt and dismantle international criminal networks that pose threats to national security and global stability. The designations aim to cut off financial support and access to the U.S. financial system for those involved in these illicit activities.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026. The settlement addresses apparent violations of various sanctions programs.

Bank of America agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability. This settlement is part of a broader enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC for anti-money laundering and sanctions law violations.
The OFAC settlement with Bank of America specifically addresses apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, ICC Designation, and Burma-related Removal
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026. This settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

In separate actions, OFAC also announced a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated General Licenses. Additionally, a Burma-related designation was removed, indicating a shift in sanctions policy concerning certain entities in Burma.

The settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics highlights OFAC's continued enforcement efforts against companies that fail to comply with U.S. sanctions laws. The ICC designation and Burma-related removal reflect the dynamic nature of U.S. foreign policy and its impact on sanctions regimes.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This action provides authorization for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing Russia sanctions programs.

General Licenses are typically issued to allow for specific types of transactions or activities that are deemed consistent with U.S. foreign policy objectives, or to mitigate unintended consequences of sanctions. The details of this new General License will provide clarity on permissible activities related to Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities involved in activities that support Iran's destabilizing behavior.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License. These measures aim to provide clarity on permissible activities while maintaining pressure on the targeted regimes.

The issuance of new and amended General Licenses often reflects OFAC's efforts to fine-tune sanctions programs, ensuring they are effective in achieving their policy goals while allowing for legitimate transactions.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11.6 Million by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a civil penalty of $11,662,930 against Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026. This penalty is part of a settlement agreement addressing apparent violations of various U.S. sanctions programs.

The enforcement action against Bank of America highlights OFAC's continued focus on ensuring compliance with sanctions regulations across the financial industry. This substantial penalty underscores the importance of robust internal controls and compliance programs to prevent sanctions breaches.

The violations involved numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism, as detailed in a broader U.S. Treasury announcement of over $1.21 billion in penalties against the bank for anti-money laundering and sanctions law violations.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has agreed to pay a civil penalty of $175,015 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), as announced on October 9, 2026. This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The penalty against Pegasus Worldwide Logistics serves as a reminder to companies involved in international trade and logistics of their obligations to comply with U.S. sanctions laws. OFAC continues to enforce these regulations to prevent illicit financial activities and support U.S. foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1.4 Million by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,427,230 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on September 10, 2026. This significant penalty underscores OFAC's commitment to enforcing U.S. sanctions laws against individuals as well as corporate entities.

The enforcement action highlights the personal responsibility individuals bear in adhering to sanctions regulations, particularly in complex financial transactions or international dealings. OFAC continues to pursue actions against those who violate these critical national security measures.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $60,764
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. has reached a settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), agreeing to pay a civil penalty of $60,764, as announced on August 12, 2026. The settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

This enforcement action serves as a reminder to companies across various industries about the importance of comprehensive sanctions compliance programs. Even smaller penalties demonstrate OFAC's broad reach and its commitment to enforcing U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Significant Enforcement Actions Against American Express National Bank and Bank of America
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today released enforcement actions for October 2026, including a Cease and Desist Order and a Civil Money Penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah. The bank was cited for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and violations related to customer due diligence and customer identification programs. The assessed civil money penalty is $350 million.

Additionally, the OCC issued a Civil Money Penalty against Bank of America, National Association, Charlotte, North Carolina, for similar deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. Bank of America was assessed a civil money penalty of $750 million.

The OCC also announced Orders of Prohibition against two institution-affiliated parties: Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at Fifth Third Bank, N.A., for embezzling approximately $292,000 in customer funds, and Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at U.S. Bank National Association, for embezzling approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Crowdfund Insider

articles.headline: OCC Report Finds Nine Major Banks Engaged in Debanking Practices
body: On October 14, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released a report titled 'Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans,' examining the debanking practices of the nine largest national banks it supervises. The report concludes that between 2020 and September 2025, each of these banks maintained policies or practices that may have led to the denial or limitation of financial services based on customers' political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities.

The OCC identified two categories of policies associated with debanking: broad reputation risk policies and industry-specific restrictions. The latter included sectors such as oil and gas exploration, coal mining, firearms and ammunition manufacturing, detention facilities, tobacco, e-cigarettes, and digital asset activities.

While the OCC did not announce any enforcement actions or penalties in this report, Comptroller Jonathan Gould stated that the OCC is 'not confident' that the banks' own remedial efforts will be sufficient and is considering further changes to the regulatory and supervisory framework. The OCC is also exploring actions to prevent discrimination based on political or religious beliefs.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Ballotpedia News

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
